This document is the R counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 09 - Algorithmic Curation and Governance](../../Notebooks/Part%2009%20-%20Algorithmic%20Curation%20and%20Governance/Part%2009%20-%20Algorithmic%20Curation%20and%20Governance.ipynb).

## Background

> **tl;dr**: On most platforms "the algorithm" is a black box you can
> only audit from the outside — or from the inside, if the platform lets
> you in. On Bluesky, feed algorithms, moderation labels, lists, and
> starter packs are *public infrastructure*: anyone can publish them and
> anyone can query them. This document treats them as objects of study,
> running a small algorithm audit that compares the composition of
> several custom feeds against a no-algorithm baseline, and then mapping
> the rest of Bluesky's governance stack.

### What is an algorithm audit?

An **algorithm audit** is a research design that treats an algorithmic
system the way investigators treat an opaque institution: probe it
systematically, record what it does, and compare its behavior against a
baseline or a standard. The name is borrowed from housing-discrimination
*audit studies*, in which matched pairs of testers applied for the same
apartment to detect differential treatment.
[Sandvig et al. (2014)](https://websites.umich.edu/~csandvig/research/Auditing%20Algorithms%20--%20Sandvig%20--%20ICA%202014%20Data%20and%20Discrimination%20Preconference.pdf)
imported the idea into platform research and catalogued the main designs
(code audits, scraping audits, sock-puppet audits, crowdsourced audits);
[Metaxa et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1561/1100000083) is a
book-length, accessible survey of the method. Keep that taxonomy in mind
— by the end of this document you will have run a *scraping audit*, and
you will understand precisely why the other designs still matter.

### Auditing the algorithm, then and now

For fifteen years, the question "what does the algorithm amplify?" could
only be answered two ways on Twitter. You could be *inside* the company:
[Huszár et al. (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2025334119) measured
the algorithmic amplification of political content by running a massive
experiment on Twitter's own servers, comparing users held on
reverse-chronological timelines against users given the algorithmic
ranking — a study design literally impossible without internal access.
Or you could probe from *outside*:
[Bandy & Diakopoulos (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3449152) built
sock-puppet accounts that followed identical sets of news sources and
recorded what the curated timeline showed them, inferring the
algorithm's behavior from its outputs. Both designs treat the ranking
system as a sealed box.

Bluesky's architecture changes the terms of this problem. The
[AT Protocol](https://atproto.com) — the open protocol Bluesky runs on —
*unbundles* curation and moderation from the platform:

* **Feed generators** are services, published as public records, that
  return a ranked list of posts — a *custom feed* is just a feed
  generator someone has published
  ([docs](https://bsky.network/docs/starter-templates/custom-feeds)).
  Anyone can publish one; anyone can request any feed's current contents
  through `app.bsky.feed.getFeed`. The Discover feed that millions of
  users see is queryable by the same endpoint as a hobbyist's feed.
* **Labelers** are independent moderation services that emit *labels*
  (like `porn`, `graphic-media`, or `!hide`) on accounts and posts
  ([docs](https://bsky.network/docs/advanced-guides/moderation)). Clients
  subscribe to labelers and decide what to do with their labels —
  Bluesky calls this
  [*stackable moderation*](https://bsky.social/about/blog/03-12-2024-stackable-moderation).
  Labels are queryable through `com.atproto.label.queryLabels`.
* **Lists** are public rosters of accounts used for curation (list
  feeds) and moderation (shared mute/block lists).
* **Starter packs** are onboarding bundles — a list of accounts plus
  optional feeds — that shape which network a newcomer lands in.

None of this makes audits trivial: as we will see, the *personalized*
layer is still invisible without logging in as a user. But the skeleton
of the curation system — what each feed serves, what each labeler flags,
who is on which list — is open to any researcher with an HTTP client.

### Learning objectives

After working through this document you will be able to:

1. Discover and describe published feed generators with
   `app.bsky.feed.getActorFeeds` and `app.bsky.feed.getFeedGenerators`.
2. Collect samples of posts from custom feeds via `app.bsky.feed.getFeed`,
   working with raw responses when typed cleaning lags behind the
   protocol.
3. Run an audit-style comparison of feed composition: author
   concentration (top-10 share, HHI, Gini), recency, engagement,
   language mix, and media share.
4. Measure audience overlap between feeds with Jaccard similarity.
5. Describe lists, starter packs, and labelers as governance
   infrastructure, and query moderation labels from a labeler service.
6. Discuss what algorithm audits can and cannot establish on a platform
   where algorithms are inspectable but personalization is private.

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)

```

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)

BSKY_APP_DID <- "did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur"  # bsky.app
BSKY_MOD_DID <- "did:plc:ar7c4by46qjdydhdevvrndac"  # moderation.bsky.app
PUBLIC_APPVIEW <- "https://public.api.bsky.app"
```

## 1. Feed generators are public records

Two pieces of AT Protocol vocabulary before we begin. A **DID**
(*decentralized identifier*, [spec](https://atproto.com/specs/did)) is an
account's permanent, machine-readable identity — a string like
`did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur` that never changes even when the
human-readable handle (`bsky.app`) does. An **AT-URI**
([spec](https://atproto.com/specs/at-uri-scheme)) is the protocol's
addressing scheme for records: `at://<DID>/<record type>/<record key>`
names one specific record in one specific account's public repository,
the way a URL names a web page.

On Bluesky, a feed algorithm is announced to the world as an
`app.bsky.feed.generator` record in its publisher's repository. Each
feed therefore has a stable AT-URI of the form
`at://<publisher DID>/app.bsky.feed.generator/<name>`, plus public
metadata: a display name, a description, and a count of users who have
liked (roughly, saved) the feed. If you have ever wondered what "the
algorithm" *is*, on this platform the answer is concrete: a record you
can look up, pointing at a service you can query.

[`app.bsky.feed.getActorFeeds`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getActorFeeds)
lists every feed generator a given account publishes; bskyr wraps it as
[`bs_get_feeds()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_feeds.html)
(each bskyr function links to its reference page on first use). Let's
start with the official `bsky.app` account, which publishes the feeds
most users encounter first — including **Discover**, the platform's
flagship algorithmic feed:

```{r actor-feeds}
bsky_feeds <- bs_get_feeds("bsky.app", limit = 50)

bsky_feeds |>
  select(display_name, like_count, description) |>
  mutate(like_count = as.integer(like_count)) |>
  arrange(desc(like_count))
```

Note how each row is an *algorithm with a public address*. Some of these
(Discover, Popular With Friends, Mutuals, Best of Follows) describe
themselves in terms of "your" network — they are personalized, a
distinction that will matter shortly.

The official account is only one publisher among thousands. Anyone can
run a feed generator, and some third-party feeds rival the official ones
in popularity.
[`bs_get_feed_generators()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_feed_generators.html)
(`app.bsky.feed.getFeedGenerators`) resolves any batch of feed URIs to
their metadata, so we can look up two well-known community feeds — the
**Science** feed (a curated feed of verified scientists, run by
`bossett.social`) and the **News** feed (headlines from verified news
organizations, run by `aendra.com`) — alongside two official ones.
Naming exactly which algorithm you sampled is part of the audit record:

```{r generators}
CANDIDATE_FEEDS <- c(
  "Discover" = paste0("at://", BSKY_APP_DID,
                      "/app.bsky.feed.generator/whats-hot"),
  "What's Hot Classic" = paste0("at://", BSKY_APP_DID,
                                "/app.bsky.feed.generator/hot-classic"),
  "Science" = "at://did:plc:jfhpnnst6flqway4eaeqzj2a/app.bsky.feed.generator/for-science",
  "News" = "at://did:plc:kkf4naxqmweop7dv4l2iqqf5/app.bsky.feed.generator/verified-news"
)

generators <- bs_get_feed_generators(unname(CANDIDATE_FEEDS))

generators |>
  select(display_name, creator_handle, like_count)
```

The AppView also offers a discovery endpoint,
[`app.bsky.feed.getSuggestedFeeds`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getSuggestedFeeds)
([`bs_get_feed_suggestions()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_feed_suggestions.html)),
which returns the feeds Bluesky would suggest to a user browsing the feed
marketplace. It is a useful way to build a sampling frame of *prominent*
feeds for a larger audit:

```{r suggested-feeds}
suggested <- tryCatch(bs_get_feed_suggestions(limit = 10),
                      error = \(e) {
                        message("getSuggestedFeeds unavailable: ", conditionMessage(e))
                        NULL
                      })

if (!is.null(suggested)) {
  suggested |>
    transmute(display_name, creator_handle, like_count = as.integer(like_count))
}
```

One feed we *cannot* observe from nowhere is the **Following** timeline
— the reverse-chronological feed of accounts a user follows. There is no
"anyone's" timeline:
[`app.bsky.feed.getTimeline`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getTimeline)
([`bs_get_timeline()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_timeline.html))
is defined relative to the logged-in account, so what it returns is *your*
Following feed, not a property of the network. This is the first
boundary of auditing from outside; we will build a reverse-chronological
baseline from a public list feed instead (Section 2):

```{r timeline}
timeline <- bs_get_timeline(limit = 5)
cat("Your own Following timeline returned", nrow(timeline),
    "posts: a view only your account can see.\n")
```

## 2. Sampling posts from custom feeds

[`app.bsky.feed.getFeed`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getFeed)
([`bs_get_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_feed.html))
returns the current contents of any published feed — the same endpoint
the official app calls when you open a feed. Before collecting in bulk,
two practical lessons learned the hard way.

**Lesson 1: personalized feeds have no "view from nowhere".** Feeds like
*Popular With Friends* rank posts relative to a specific viewer. With no
viewer, the feed generator simply errors out — there is no answer to
"popular with *whose* friends?". When you run this document logged in,
the feed is ranked relative to *your* account instead, which is a
different object from what anyone else sees. Watch what happens:

```{r personalized-feed}
with_friends <- paste0("at://", BSKY_APP_DID, "/app.bsky.feed.generator/with-friends")

tryCatch({
  personal <- bs_get_feed(with_friends, limit = 5)
  cat("Popular With Friends returned", nrow(personal), "posts, ranked relative",
      "to *your* account:\nno one else would see this list.\n")
}, error = \(e) {
  cat("The 'Popular With Friends' feed generator refused the request:",
      conditionMessage(e), "\n")
  cat("Personalized feeds are only observable from the standpoint of a particular",
      "user -\nexactly the layer Huszar et al. (2022) needed internal access to study.\n")
})
```

**Lesson 2: lexicons evolve faster than software.** A **lexicon** is AT
Protocol's schema language ([guide](https://atproto.com/guides/lexicon)):
every record type (`app.bsky.feed.post`), embed type
(`app.bsky.embed.images`), and API method (`app.bsky.feed.getFeed`) is
defined by a published lexicon schema, named by a reverse-domain
identifier. The network can mint new lexicon types at any time — and
software that has not heard of them yet must cope. (While developing the
Python version, a then-new `app.bsky.embed.gallery` type crashed the
SDK's parser.) So, as in Part 07, we take the raw response
(`clean = FALSE`) and flatten just the fields the audit needs ourselves.
`classify_embed()` mirrors the Python helper: it names the embed type and
decides whether the post carries images or video, including posts that
pair media with a quote (`recordWithMedia`) and multi-image `gallery`
posts.

Note the bookkeeping that makes an audit an audit: every sample records
*when it was retrieved*, because a feed is a moving target and "the
Discover feed" without a timestamp is not a defined object. And note the
`tryCatch()` around each feed: these are live third-party services that
can error or vanish, and a resilient audit pipeline skips a dead feed
rather than crashing. Let's pull roughly **150 posts from each of our
four candidate feeds**:

```{r fetch-feeds}
classify_embed <- function(embed) {
  if (is.null(embed)) return(list(type = NA_character_, media = FALSE))
  type <- str_remove_all(embed$`$type` %||% "", "app\\.bsky\\.embed\\.|#view")
  media <- if (type == "recordWithMedia") {
    str_detect(embed$media$`$type` %||% "", "images|video")
  } else {
    type %in% c("images", "video", "gallery")
  }
  list(type = type, media = media)
}

flatten_post <- function(item) {
  post <- item$post
  record <- post$record %||% list()
  embed <- classify_embed(post$embed)
  tibble(
    uri = post$uri,
    author_did = post$author$did,
    author_handle = post$author$handle %||% NA_character_,
    created_at = record$createdAt %||% NA_character_,
    like_count = post$likeCount %||% 0L,
    repost_count = post$repostCount %||% 0L,
    reply_count = post$replyCount %||% 0L,
    quote_count = post$quoteCount %||% 0L,
    lang = unlist(record$langs)[1] %||% NA_character_,
    embed_type = embed$type,
    has_media = embed$media,
    text_chars = nchar(record$text %||% ""),
    via_repost = !is.null(item$reason)
  )
}

flatten_pages <- function(pages) {
  map(list_flatten(map(pages, "feed")), flatten_post) |> list_rbind()
}

feed_posts <- function(uri, target = 150) {
  pages <- tryCatch(bs_get_feed(uri, limit = target, clean = FALSE),
                    error = function(e) {
                      message("skipped ", uri, ": ", conditionMessage(e))
                      NULL
                    })
  if (is.null(pages)) NULL else flatten_pages(pages)
}

samples <- imap(CANDIDATE_FEEDS, \(uri, name) {
  retrieved_at <- now("UTC")
  posts <- feed_posts(uri)
  Sys.sleep(0.5)
  if (is.null(posts)) return(NULL)
  mutate(posts, feed = name, retrieved_at = retrieved_at)
})

map_int(compact(samples), nrow)
```

### A no-algorithm baseline

Huszár et al. (2022) could compare algorithmic timelines against users
held on reverse-chronological ones. Our public analogue is a **list
feed**:
[`app.bsky.feed.getListFeed`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getListFeed)
([`bs_get_list_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_list_feed.html))
returns the posts of a list's members in pure reverse-chronological
order — no ranking model at all. We find the official `bsky.app`
account's curation list with
[`bs_get_actor_lists()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_actor_lists.html)
(we examine lists properly in Section 5) and use it as a fixed roster,
giving us a "what does no algorithm look like?" comparison sample.

This baseline is not a perfect stand-in for a Following timeline — its
roster is small and curated by Bluesky — but it isolates the property we
care about: *chronology versus ranking*.

```{r baseline}
bsky_lists <- bs_get_actor_lists("bsky.app", limit = 50) |>
  bsky_standardize()   # same column names under bskyr 0.4.x and 0.5.0

baseline_list <- bsky_lists |>
  filter(str_detect(purpose, "curatelist")) |>
  slice_head(n = 1)

baseline_posts <- NULL
if (nrow(baseline_list) == 1) {
  cat("Baseline roster:", baseline_list$name, "(",
      as.integer(baseline_list$list_item_count), "members )\n")
  retrieved_at <- now("UTC")
  baseline_posts <- bs_get_list_feed(baseline_list$uri, limit = 150, clean = FALSE) |>
    flatten_pages() |>
    mutate(feed = "Baseline (list feed)", retrieved_at = retrieved_at)
}
```

### Flattening into a tidy archive

`flatten_post()` turned each nested feed item into one row of
*audit-relevant* fields: who posted, when, engagement counts, declared
language, and embed/media type. We now stack the samples, drop duplicate
posts within a feed, and compute each post's **age at retrieval**.
Client-supplied `createdAt` timestamps are occasionally bogus
(future-dated), so negative ages become missing rather than distorting
the recency measures.

Notice what we deliberately do **not** keep: the post text (only its
length). A composition audit asks *who and what kind*, not *what was
said*, and the data-minimization principle from Part 01 says you should
not collect fields your research question does not require — every
column you store is a column you are responsible for.

```{r tidy-archive}
# list_rbind() stacks a list of tibbles; compact() drops feeds that failed
posts_df <- list_rbind(compact(c(samples, list(baseline_posts)))) |>
  distinct(feed, uri, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(created_at = ymd_hms(created_at, quiet = TRUE),
         age_hours = as.numeric(difftime(retrieved_at, created_at, units = "hours")),
         age_hours = if_else(age_hours >= 0, age_hours, NA_real_))

cat(nrow(posts_df), "posts across", n_distinct(posts_df$feed), "feeds\n")
count(posts_df, feed)
```

We save the archive immediately, before any analysis. Saving first is
audit hygiene: the feeds will have moved on by tomorrow, but this
snapshot, stamped with its retrieval times, is now frozen evidence that
any collaborator can reanalyze (Section 8). RDS keeps R's column types
(including the timestamps) exactly; the CSV is for everyone else:

```{r save-archive}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(posts_df, "data/feed_posts.rds")
write_csv(posts_df, "data/feed_posts.csv")
```

## 3. Auditing feed composition

Now the centerpiece: what does each algorithm actually *serve*?
Following the logic of Bandy & Diakopoulos (2021) — characterize the
curated output and compare it against a chronological counterfactual —
we compute a panel of composition metrics per feed:

* **Author concentration.** Does the feed amplify a few voices or many?
  We use three complementary measures of the distribution of posts over
  authors: the share contributed by the **top 10 authors**, the
  **Herfindahl–Hirschman index** (the economists' market-concentration
  measure: the sum of squared author shares, $\mathrm{HHI} = \sum_i s_i^2$,
  where $1/n$ means perfectly even and 1 means a single author), and the
  **Gini coefficient** (0 = every author contributes equally, → 1 =
  maximal inequality).
* **Recency.** The median and 90th-percentile *age* of posts at the
  moment we retrieved them. A trending algorithm should serve hours-old
  posts; a sparse chronological roster may surface much older ones.
* **Engagement.** Median and 90th-percentile like counts. Ranked feeds
  that select on popularity should show dramatically higher engagement
  than a feed that selects on time alone — selection, not causation!
* **Language mix and media share.** What fraction of posts declare
  English, how many languages appear, and how often posts carry images
  or video.

```{r composition}
gini <- function(counts) {
  values <- sort(as.numeric(counts))
  n <- length(values)
  if (n == 0 || sum(values) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  cumulative <- cumsum(values)
  (n + 1 - 2 * sum(cumulative / cumulative[n])) / n
}

hhi <- function(counts) {
  shares <- as.numeric(counts) / sum(counts)
  sum(shares^2)
}

top_k_share <- function(counts, k = 10) {
  sum(head(sort(as.numeric(counts), decreasing = TRUE), k)) / sum(counts)
}

comparison <- posts_df |>
  group_by(feed) |>
  summarise(
    posts = n(),
    unique_authors = n_distinct(author_did),
    top10_author_share = top_k_share(table(author_did)),
    author_hhi = hhi(table(author_did)),
    author_gini = gini(table(author_did)),
    median_age_hours = median(age_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    p90_age_hours = quantile(age_hours, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
    median_likes = median(like_count),
    p90_likes = quantile(like_count, 0.9, names = FALSE),
    share_english = mean(lang %in% "en"),
    n_languages = n_distinct(lang, na.rm = TRUE),
    media_share = mean(has_media),
    median_text_chars = median(text_chars)
  )

write_csv(comparison, "data/feed_comparison.csv")
comparison |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

Tables reward close reading, but the contrasts jump out in small-multiple
charts. The top row shows **empirical cumulative distribution functions
(ECDFs)**: for each value $x$ on the horizontal axis, the curve's height
is the share of the feed's posts at or below $x$ — so read a point on
the recency curve as "this fraction of the feed is younger than $x$
hours." ECDFs beat histograms for comparing skewed distributions because
every post is shown and no binning choices intervene. Both use log
scales (Part 04 taught us engagement is heavy-tailed), and the bottom
row uses simple bars for concentration and media share. patchwork's `+`
and `/` operators arrange the four ggplots into one figure, and
`plot_layout(guides = "collect")` gives them a single shared legend:

```{r composition-plots, fig.width=11, fig.height=8}
feed_levels <- comparison$feed

recency <- posts_df |>
  filter(age_hours > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(age_hours, color = feed)) +
  stat_ecdf() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(drop0trailing = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "Post age at retrieval (hours)", y = "Cumulative share of posts",
       title = "Recency profile", color = "Feed")

engagement <- ggplot(posts_df, aes(like_count + 1, color = feed)) +
  stat_ecdf() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Likes at retrieval (+1)", y = "Cumulative share of posts",
       title = "Engagement profile", color = "Feed")

concentration <- ggplot(comparison, aes(top10_author_share,
                                        fct_rev(factor(feed, feed_levels)), fill = feed)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Share of posts from top 10 authors", y = NULL,
       title = "Author concentration")

media <- ggplot(comparison, aes(media_share,
                                fct_rev(factor(feed, feed_levels)), fill = feed)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Share of posts with images or video", y = NULL,
       title = "Media share")

(recency + engagement) / (concentration + media) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(title = "Composition of Bluesky feeds") &
  theme_minimal()
```

Before interpreting, let's pull the four contrasts we care most about
into one small table: each feed's median likes (and how many times the
baseline's that is, with +1 smoothing so a baseline median of 0 can't
divide by zero), its median post age, its top-10 author share, and how
many distinct authors it drew on:

```{r contrasts}
baseline_likes <- comparison$median_likes[comparison$feed == "Baseline (list feed)"]

comparison |>
  transmute(feed, median_likes, median_age_hours = round(median_age_hours, 2),
            top10_author_share = round(top10_author_share, 2), unique_authors,
            likes_vs_baseline = if (length(baseline_likes) == 1)
              round((median_likes + 1) / (baseline_likes + 1), 2) else NA_real_)
```

### What the differences reveal

Your numbers will differ from ours — these are live feeds — so read the
magnitudes from the table above rather than from this text. What *is*
stable is the logic behind each contrast, and each one tells you
something about how the feed curates:

* **Engagement depends on what a feed selects on.** Discover and What's
  Hot Classic rank posts by popularity signals, so their posts' like
  counts sit above the chronological baseline's — usually far above, in
  Discover's case. Nothing about the algorithm *caused* that engagement;
  the feed conditions on it. This is the selection effect that makes
  naive "posts on the algorithmic feed get more likes!" claims circular.
  The allowlist feeds (Science, News) work differently: they admit posts
  from a vetted roster of accounts rather than ranking the whole network
  by popularity, so their median likes can sit near, or even below, the
  baseline's. An "algorithmic" feed is not necessarily an
  engagement-ranked one; check what a feed selects on before comparing
  engagement across feeds.
* **Recency is a design choice.** Some feeds serve posts only minutes
  old; others serve posts a few hours old, as a trending feed does while
  it waits for engagement to accumulate; all of them filter out
  staleness with a sharp upper bound (compare the `p90_age_hours`
  column). The chronological baseline's age profile, by contrast, is
  just the posting rhythm of its roster: if the roster is quiet, the
  feed reaches days into the past.
* **Concentration reflects the eligible population.** Allowlist feeds
  draw from a vetted roster, so a handful of prolific accounts can
  supply a large share of their posts. A network-wide feed samples from
  millions of eligible authors, so a single snapshot tends to spread
  across more of them. The baseline is the extreme case: its roster is
  the handful of members printed in Section 2, so its concentration is
  high by construction. Concentration metrics are only comparable across
  feeds with similar eligible populations — a classic denominator
  subtlety.
* **Language and media mixes expose filters and incentives.** A feed's
  English share and media share tell you whether it filters by language
  or rewards visual content. One measurement caveat: `lang` is
  *self-declared* by posting clients, and institutional accounts — like
  the news organizations here — often omit it, so a low `share_english`
  can mean undeclared rather than non-English. Differences in exposure
  like these are what Bandy & Diakopoulos (2021) showed can meaningfully
  reshape the news users encounter.

## 4. Audience overlap between feeds

Do these feeds amplify the *same people*? For each pair of feeds we
compute the **Jaccard similarity** of their author sets:

$$J(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}$$

which is 0 when two feeds share no authors and 1 when they amplify
identical sets. tidyr's `crossing()` builds every pair of feeds. We write
`tidyr::crossing()` with the package name because igraph, which Parts 03
and 04 load, has a different function also called `crossing()`; if
igraph is still attached in your R session, the plain name would call
the wrong one:

```{r jaccard}
author_sets <- posts_df |>
  group_by(feed) |>
  summarise(authors = list(unique(author_did)))

jaccard <- function(a, b) length(intersect(a, b)) / length(union(a, b))

overlap <- tidyr::crossing(f1 = author_sets$feed, f2 = author_sets$feed) |>
  mutate(jaccard = map2_dbl(
    f1, f2,
    \(x, y) jaccard(author_sets$authors[[match(x, author_sets$feed)]],
                    author_sets$authors[[match(y, author_sets$feed)]])
  ))

overlap |>
  mutate(jaccard = round(jaccard, 3)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = f2, values_from = jaccard)
```

A pairwise matrix is easier to scan as a heatmap. Each cell is the
Jaccard similarity between the author sets of the row feed and the
column feed; the diagonal is 1 by definition (every feed overlaps
perfectly with itself), and we annotate each cell with its value so you
do not have to squint at the color scale. The color scale stops at the
largest *off-diagonal* value (or 0.10, if that is larger), so the
diagonal's 1s don't wash out the small overlaps that matter:

```{r jaccard-heatmap, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.5}
top_off_diagonal <- max(c(0.10, overlap$jaccard[overlap$f1 != overlap$f2]))

ggplot(overlap, aes(f2, f1, fill = jaccard)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", jaccard),
                color = jaccard > top_off_diagonal / 2), size = 3.2,
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "black", `FALSE` = "white")) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Jaccard\nsimilarity", limits = c(0, top_off_diagonal),
                       oob = scales::squish) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Jaccard overlap of author sets between feeds") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

The headline finding is usually how *small* these overlaps are: in a
single snapshot, each feed amplifies a nearly disjoint set of authors.
Custom feeds are not five windows onto one conversation — they carve the
network into largely separate audiences and speaker populations. (Which
cells are nonzero, and by how much, will fluctuate between runs; even
the largest overlaps in a snapshot tend to be a small fraction of either
feed's authors.)

For a research design, this is the dependent variable in miniature:
*exposure diversity*. With repeated snapshots you could ask whether
feeds' author populations churn or ossify over time, and whose voices
never appear in any algorithmic feed at all.

## 5. Lists: shared rosters for curation and moderation

Lists are the simplest governance object on Bluesky: a public, named
roster of accounts (`app.bsky.graph.list` records). One mechanism, two
very different uses, distinguished by the record's `purpose` field:

* **`curatelist`** — content curation: a list feed (as in our baseline),
  or a roster to pin and browse.
* **`modlist`** — moderation: users who subscribe to a moderation list
  can mute or block *every member at once*. Shared blocklists, which
  emerged on Twitter as a grassroots harassment defense, are first-class
  protocol objects here.
* **`referencelist`** — internal rosters referenced by other records
  (starter packs use these).

[`app.bsky.graph.getLists`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskygraph/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.graph.getLists)
enumerates an account's published lists (we already called it, through
`bs_get_actor_lists()`, to find our baseline):

```{r lists}
bsky_lists |>
  transmute(name, purpose = str_extract(purpose, "[^#]+$"),
            members = as.integer(list_item_count),
            description = str_trunc(replace_na(description, ""), 80))
```

Who is actually *on* a list?
[`app.bsky.graph.getList`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskygraph/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.graph.getList)
pages through a list's members with the same cursor pattern as every
other paginated endpoint in this series;
[`bs_get_list()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_list.html)
follows the cursor for us up to the `limit` we set (our cap, as always).
Let's unpack the curation list we used as our chronological baseline in
Section 2, so we can see exactly whose posts that baseline sample
contained:

```{r list-members}
if (nrow(baseline_list) == 1) {
  members <- bs_get_list(baseline_list$uri, limit = 200)
  cat(baseline_list$name, "has", nrow(members), "members\n")
  members |> select(subject_handle, subject_display_name) |> head(10)
}
```

Membership on a list is consequential and *non-consensual*: accounts do
not opt in to being listed, and inclusion on a widely-subscribed
moderation list can silently sever someone from a large audience. That
makes lists a rich research site — who maintains influential modlists,
how membership changes over time, what the error rates look like — and
also a sensitive one: a dataset of "accounts on blocklist X" is
effectively an accusation attached to identities. Aggregate analyses are
usually the right level of reporting.

## 6. Starter packs: curating the network itself

Starter packs (`app.bsky.graph.starterpack` records) bundle a reference
list of accounts — and optionally feeds — into a shareable onboarding
page. A newcomer who joins through a starter pack can follow everyone on
it with one tap. Where feeds curate *content*, starter packs curate the
*follow graph*: they decide which corner of the network a new user lands
in.

[`app.bsky.graph.getActorStarterPacks`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskygraph/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.graph.getActorStarterPacks)
([`bs_get_actor_starter_packs()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_actor_starter_packs.html))
lists an account's packs with counts of how many users joined through
each, this week and all time. This summary view doesn't say how many
accounts each pack contains; to see a pack's members we fetch the pack
itself, as we do for one pack below. `bsky_standardize()` from
`bsky_client.R` gives the count columns the same names whichever bskyr
version you have installed:

```{r starter-packs}
packs <- bs_get_actor_starter_packs("bsky.app", limit = 50) |>
  bsky_standardize() |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("joined"), as.integer))   # counts can arrive as text

cat(nrow(packs), "starter packs published by bsky.app\n")
packs |>
  transmute(name = record_name, joined_this_week = joined_week_count,
            joined_all_time = joined_all_time_count,
            created = as.Date(substr(record_created_at, 1, 10)))
```

Notice the editorial rhythm: the official account spins up packs around
scheduled events — elections, playoffs, award shows — pre-assembling an
audience for each. Let's unpack one. A starter pack's accounts live in an
ordinary reference list, so we fetch the pack with
[`app.bsky.graph.getStarterPack`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskygraph/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.graph.getStarterPack)
([`bs_get_starter_pack()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_starter_pack.html),
raw, because its cleaned form flattens the embedded feed list into
dozens of columns) and then read its list members with the same
`bs_get_list()` call as before:

```{r starter-pack-unpack}
# The pack the most users have actually joined through
top_pack <- packs |> slice_max(joined_all_time_count, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
pack_view <- bs_get_starter_pack(top_pack$uri, clean = FALSE)$starterPack

cat("Starter pack:", pack_view$record$name, "\n")
cat("Description: ", str_trunc(pack_view$record$description %||% "(none)", 100), "\n")
cat("Joined through it:", pack_view$joinedAllTimeCount %||% 0, "accounts all-time\n")

if (!is.null(pack_view$list)) {
  pack_members <- bs_get_list(pack_view$list$uri, limit = 100)
  cat("Accounts in the pack:", nrow(pack_members), "\n")
  pack_members |> select(subject_handle, subject_display_name) |> head(10)
} else {
  cat("This pack has no account list attached.\n")
}
```

### Starter packs as a natural experiment

For network science, starter packs are a gift: a *measurable treatment*
in network formation. Two users who join Bluesky in the same week
through different starter packs receive different initial follow
neighborhoods — assigned largely by whichever link happened to reach
them, not by slowly homegrown homophily. Because pack membership, join
counts, and the full follow graph (Part 03) are all public, you can ask
classic questions with unusual leverage:

* Do users seeded into different packs end up in durably different
  communities, or does organic rewiring wash out the initial conditions?
* How much of an account's long-run audience traces back to
  starter-pack placement — a *Matthew effect* with an observable origin?
* Do packs accelerate the early-follower accumulation that Part 04's
  diffusion models treat as exogenous?

The identification is not free — who joins through which pack is not
random — but compared with inferring initial conditions retrospectively,
an explicit, timestamped onboarding bundle is about as close to a
natural experiment in network formation as platforms provide.

## 7. Labels and stackable moderation

The third leg of Bluesky's governance stack is moderation. Instead of
one company applying one policy, AT Protocol moderation is performed by
**labelers**: independent services that publish *labels* — small signed
records attaching a value like `porn`, `graphic-media`, `rude`, or the
hide-everything `!takedown` — to accounts, posts, and other records (see
the [moderation architecture docs](https://bsky.network/docs/advanced-guides/moderation)).
Users subscribe to labelers (Bluesky's own labeler is just the default
subscription), and each client decides how to render each label: hide,
warn, badge, or ignore. This is what Bluesky calls **stackable
moderation** — many overlapping moderation authorities instead of one —
introduced in the blog post
["Bluesky's Stackable Approach to Moderation"](https://bsky.social/about/blog/03-12-2024-stackable-moderation),
which is worth reading in full as a design statement about who should
hold moderation power.

Crucially for researchers, labelers are *queryable services*. First,
let's read the Bluesky Moderation Service's public "policy menu" — the
set of label values it may emit — via
[`app.bsky.labeler.getServices`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskylabeler/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.labeler.getServices).
bskyr has no wrapper for this endpoint or for label queries, which is a
teachable moment in itself: any XRPC endpoint is just an HTTP URL, so we
build the request directly with httr2. `getServices` is a public read,
so we send it to the public AppView with no login at all:

```{r labeler-services}
services <- tryCatch(
  httr2::request(paste0(PUBLIC_APPVIEW, "/xrpc/app.bsky.labeler.getServices")) |>
    httr2::req_url_query(dids = BSKY_MOD_DID, detailed = "true") |>
    httr2::req_perform() |>
    httr2::resp_body_json(),
  error = \(e) {
    message("getServices unavailable: ", conditionMessage(e))
    NULL
  })

if (!is.null(services) && length(services$views) > 0) {
  service_view <- services$views[[1]]
  cat("Labeler:", service_view$creator$handle, "(", service_view$creator$did, ")\n")
  cat("Liked (subscribed) by", format(service_view$likeCount, big.mark = ","), "accounts\n\n")
  cat("Label values this service may emit:\n")
  cat(str_wrap(paste(unlist(service_view$policies$labelValues), collapse = ", "), 80), "\n")
}
```

Now the audit question: **do any of the posts our feeds served carry
moderation labels?** The Bluesky Moderation Service answers
[`com.atproto.label.queryLabels`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/comatprotolabel/GET/xrpc/com.atproto.label.queryLabels)
at `https://mod.bsky.app`. Our `query_labels()` sends the patterns in
batches of 25 per request, pauses between requests, caps the number of
requests, and collects the labels from every batch into one tibble. We
query the exact URIs of up to 300 posts from our archive.

One design choice deserves attention before we use it: if the labeler
**refuses** a request, the function stops with an error that carries the
labeler's own explanation, instead of quietly returning an empty table.
A refused request and a request that found nothing both "return no
labels", but only one of them is a finding. Code that blurs the two
produces confident, wrong conclusions — exactly what happened to an
earlier version of this document, as the next chunks show.
`httr2::req_error(body = ...)` is what pulls the server's message into
the error:

```{r labels}
query_labels <- function(patterns, labeler = "https://mod.bsky.app",
                         batch_size = 25, max_requests = 20) {
  batches <- split(patterns, ceiling(seq_along(patterns) / batch_size))
  if (length(batches) > max_requests) {
    message("Querying only the first ", max_requests, " of ",
            length(batches), " batches")
    batches <- head(batches, max_requests)
  }
  labels <- list()
  for (i in seq_along(batches)) {
    resp <- httr2::request(paste0(labeler, "/xrpc/com.atproto.label.queryLabels")) |>
      httr2::req_url_query(uriPatterns = batches[[i]], limit = 250, .multi = "explode") |>
      httr2::req_error(body = \(r) c(
        tryCatch(httr2::resp_body_json(r)$message, error = \(e) NULL),
        sprintf("(%s refused label query batch %d of %d)", labeler, i, length(batches))
      )) |>
      httr2::req_perform() |>
      httr2::resp_body_json()
    labels <- c(labels, resp$labels)
    Sys.sleep(0.2)
  }
  tibble(uri = map_chr(labels, "uri"),
         val = map_chr(labels, "val"),
         neg = map_lgl(labels, \(l) isTRUE(l$neg)))
}

post_uris <- head(unique(posts_df$uri), 300)
post_labels <- query_labels(post_uris)
cat("Queried", length(post_uris), "post URIs from our feed samples ->",
    nrow(post_labels), "labels found\n")
post_labels |> count(val, sort = TRUE)
```

Labels are usually sparse on curated-feed posts, because curation and
moderation interact: most labeled content never *reaches* a feed, and
what the AppView has taken down we never see at all. When some labels do
appear (often adult-content labels on posts from the open trending
feeds), notice what that teaches: a label does not delete anything. The
post sits in the feed's public skeleton *with its label attached*, and
each user's client decides — based on their labeler subscriptions and
preferences — whether to hide, blur, or show it. Moderation here is
metadata, not removal.

To confirm the labeler is far from idle, we'd like to widen the query to
the *accounts* that wrote these posts. The `queryLabels` lexicon allows
wildcard patterns like `at://did:plc:.../*`, meaning "any record in this
account's history", and an earlier version of this document used
exactly that. Let's see what the moderation service says to one today.
`tryCatch()` catches the error so that we can print it rather than stop
the document:

```{r wildcard-demo}
example_did <- posts_df$author_did[1]

tryCatch({
  wildcard <- query_labels(paste0("at://", example_did, "/*"))
  cat("Wildcard queries work again:", nrow(wildcard), "labels in one account history.\n")
}, error = \(e) cat(conditionMessage(e), "\n"))
```

In 2026 Bluesky's moderation service stopped accepting wildcard queries,
answering every one with *"Support for wildcard label queries is
temporarily disabled"*. (If the chunk above reports that they work
again, the service has re-enabled them; the rest of this section works
either way.) This is the "platform in flux" lesson in its purest form:
nothing in our code changed, and the
[API reference for `queryLabels`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/comatprotolabel/GET/xrpc/com.atproto.label.queryLabels)
still describes wildcards, but a measurement that worked one month
stopped working the next. The earlier version of this document didn't
check, and reported **"No labels found in this sample"** — a confident
empirical claim produced by a refused request. That is why
`query_labels()` now stops with the server's message instead.

So we ask the questions that *can* still be asked, with two kinds of
pattern the service accepts:

* **(a) Labels on the accounts themselves.** A bare DID as the pattern
  returns labels applied to the account, as opposed to any one of its
  posts.
* **(b) Labels on their recent posts.** For 20 of the sampled authors we
  fetch their latest 30 feed items with
  [`bs_get_author_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_author_feed.html),
  keep the original posts (the `is_repost()` and `is_reply()` helpers
  from `bsky_client.R`), and query those exact URIs. This covers only a
  recent window rather than a whole history, so its counts are lower
  bounds on what a full history would show.

```{r history-labels}
set.seed(42)
sampled_dids <- sample(unique(posts_df$author_did),
                       min(50, n_distinct(posts_df$author_did)))

# (a) one bare DID per pattern
account_labels <- query_labels(sampled_dids) |> filter(!neg)  # drop retracted labels

# (b) exact URIs of recent original posts by 20 of those authors
recent_uris <- map(head(sampled_dids, 20), \(did) {
  feed <- tryCatch(bs_get_author_feed(did, limit = 30),
                   error = \(e) NULL)   # a deleted or suspended account has no feed
  Sys.sleep(0.1)
  if (is.null(feed) || nrow(feed) == 0) return(character())
  feed$uri[!is_repost(feed) & !is_reply(feed)]
}) |> list_c()
recent_labels <- query_labels(recent_uris, max_requests = 40) |> filter(!neg)

cat("(a) Labels on the", length(sampled_dids), "sampled accounts:", nrow(account_labels), "\n")
account_labels |> count(val, sort = TRUE)
cat("(b) Labels on", length(recent_uris), "recent posts by 20 authors:", nrow(recent_labels), "\n")
recent_labels |> count(val, sort = TRUE)

# Put the post samples on a common scale: active labels per 100 posts
per_100 <- function(labels, n_posts) if (n_posts > 0) 100 * sum(!labels$neg) / n_posts else NA_real_
c(feed_posts = per_100(post_labels, length(post_uris)),
  authors_recent_posts = per_100(recent_labels, length(recent_uris))) |> round(1)
```

Compare the two rates in the last line, and notice how few labels sit
behind each. With a few hundred posts and labels this sparse, a handful
of labeled posts decides which rate is higher, and reruns come out both
ways — so the comparison is a design for a study, not yet a finding
(Exercise 3 asks you to scale it up). Two things *are* stable. The
account-level labels are a different kind of judgment altogether: flags
about an account rather than about any one post. And the post labels
that do appear are mostly content-classification labels such as
`sexual`, `porn`, and `graphic-media`, which drive the client-side
warnings users configure rather than removing anything. The two-step
pattern used here (exact URIs for your sample; account DIDs and
recent-post URIs for context) is a reusable template for studying
*label prevalence*: which kinds of accounts and content get labeled, by
which labelers, and how labels and algorithmic amplification interact.

A caution before you build that study: labels are moderation *actions*,
and a row like "account X was labeled `rude`" is an allegation attached
to an identity. Report prevalence in aggregate, and remember that
third-party labelers vary enormously in standards and accountability.

## 8. Reproducibility: working from the saved archive

Both artifacts of our audit are on disk — `data/feed_posts.rds` (one
slim row per post, including its retrieval timestamp) and
`data/feed_comparison.csv` (the metric table). Every analysis from
Section 3 on can be rerun *from the files* without touching the network,
which is how you should hand an audit to a collaborator: the feeds will
have moved on, but your snapshot is frozen and documented:

```{r reload}
archive <- readRDS("data/feed_posts.rds")
saved_comparison <- read_csv("data/feed_comparison.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

cat("Reloaded", nrow(archive), "posts; collected on",
    format(min(as_date(archive$retrieved_at))), "(UTC)\n")

# A reanalysis straight from disk: engagement by feed
archive |>
  group_by(feed) |>
  summarise(median_likes = median(like_count),
            median_reposts = median(repost_count))
```

## 9. Research design: algorithm audits without platform cooperation

Step back and compare the designs available to you here against the
Twitter-era studies we started from:

* **Huszár et al. (2022)** needed Twitter's own servers and a years-long
  holdback experiment to compare algorithmic against chronological
  timelines. On Bluesky, the *public skeleton* of that comparison — what
  each published algorithm serves versus a chronological feed — took us
  well under a hundred HTTP requests. No permission, no NDA, no special
  access.
* **Bandy & Diakopoulos (2021)** had to build sock puppets to observe
  curated timelines from outside. On Bluesky the equivalent observation
  is an endpoint. But their problem has not disappeared — it has moved.
  What we audited is the **feed skeleton**: the generic,
  viewer-independent output. A logged-in user's Discover feed is
  personalized, and *that* layer is exactly as invisible to us as
  Twitter's timeline was. Sock-puppet designs (consented panels of real
  users donating their feed views, or instrumented research accounts)
  remain necessary to study personalization, and Bluesky's open protocol
  makes such panels far easier to instrument.
* **The governance stack is itself a study population.** Thousands of
  feed generators, labelers, lists, and starter packs — each with public
  metadata, subscriber counts, and queryable outputs — form an ecosystem
  of *competing curation and moderation authorities*. Who runs them?
  Which gain audiences? Do third-party labelers converge with or diverge
  from the platform's own decisions? Does stackable moderation actually
  redistribute governance power, or does everyone stay on the defaults?
  These questions have no Twitter-era analogue, because the
  infrastructure they ask about did not exist.

The general lesson: on an open protocol, the unit of audit shifts from
"the algorithm" to *an ecology of algorithms*, and the scarce resource
shifts from access to **design** — choosing baselines, denominators, and
snapshots that make the comparison meaningful.

## Ethics and limitations

**Ethics.** Everything we queried is public infrastructure, but the
people inside it did not opt into research. Posts surfaced by feeds,
accounts on lists, and labeled records all belong to users who mostly do
not know these endpoints exist. We practiced minimization (no post text
in the archive — our composition questions did not need it), reported
labels and list memberships in aggregate rather than naming accounts,
and capped every collection loop. Moderation data deserves extra care:
labels and modlist memberships are accusations as well as data points,
and republishing them attached to identities can amplify the very harms
moderation tries to contain. And remember that feed *publishers* are
people too — small hobbyist feeds can identify their one maintainer.

**Limitations.** Our audit observed each feed once. That means: (1)
**no personalization** — we saw the generic skeleton, not what any
actual user sees, and for feeds like Discover the personalized layer may
dominate; (2) **single snapshot** — feeds are moving targets, and one
retrieval confounds the algorithm with the moment (a serious audit
repeats collection across times of day and weeks); (3) **selection, not
effects** — composition differences show what feeds *select*, not what
they *cause*; engagement comparisons especially are selection effects by
construction; (4) **survivorship** — the AppView already filters
taken-down and blocked content before we see it, which is part of why
labels are sparse on the posts the feeds served; (5) **a platform in
flux** — feed rosters, labeler policies, and even lexicon types (a
brand-new embed type broke the Python SDK, and a moderation service
stopped answering wildcard label queries) change continuously, which is
why the archive records its collection timestamps and why your numbers
will not match ours.

## Exercises

The exercises below extend the document, roughly in increasing order of
effort.

1. **Add another feed to the audit.** Pick a popular community feed
   (browse the `bs_get_feed_suggestions()` output from Section 1, or the
   Feeds tab in the app) and add it to `CANDIDATE_FEEDS`, then rerun
   Sections 2–4. A feed's page URL
   `https://bsky.app/profile/<handle>/feed/<rkey>` maps to the AT-URI
   `at://<DID>/app.bsky.feed.generator/<rkey>`; resolve the handle to a
   DID with
   [`bs_resolve_handle()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_resolve_handle.html).
   How does the newcomer's composition profile compare?
2. **Bigger samples.** Raise `target` from 150 to 500 in `feed_posts()`
   and recompute the composition table. Which metrics are stable and
   which shift? Concentration measures like Gini and HHI are sensitive
   to sample size (more posts means more chances for rare authors to
   appear), so this exercise doubles as a lesson in not comparing
   concentration across samples of different sizes.
3. **Compare label prevalence across feeds.** Section 7 pooled all post
   URIs into one label query. Instead, group `posts_df` by feed, query
   labels separately for each feed's URIs (and its authors' recent
   posts), and report labels per 100 posts per feed. Do allowlist-style
   feeds (Science, News) have cleaner histories than the open trending
   feeds?
4. **Track one feed's composition across a day.** Rerun the Section 2
   collection for a single feed every few hours, appending each snapshot
   (the `retrieved_at` column already distinguishes them) to a growing
   RDS file. Plot median post age, median likes, and top-10 author share
   over the day — is the feed's character stable, or does it breathe
   with the diurnal cycle from Part 05?
5. **Author churn between snapshots.** With two snapshots of the same
   feed from Exercise 4, compute the Jaccard similarity of the feed's
   author set *with itself across time*. High self-overlap means the
   feed amplifies a stable cast; low self-overlap means it churns.
   Compare churn between an algorithmic feed and the chronological
   baseline.
6. **Starter-pack roster overlap.** Fetch the member lists of several of
   `bsky.app`'s starter packs (Section 6) and compute pairwise Jaccard
   overlap between their rosters, reusing `jaccard()` from Section 4. Do
   the packs partition accounts into disjoint bundles, or is there a
   core of accounts the platform inserts into every newcomer's network?

## Research project ideas

**1. A longitudinal audit of the feed marketplace.** *Question:* do
popular custom feeds diversify exposure relative to the official
Discover feed, or do they converge on the same engagement-bait
equilibrium? *Data:* daily snapshots, over four to eight weeks, of the
top ~25 feeds from `getSuggestedFeeds` plus Discover — composition
metrics and author sets per feed per day, collected with the resilient
pipeline from Section 2. *Method:* model each composition metric as a
panel (feed × day), compare ranked feeds against chronological list-feed
baselines, and track exposure diversity as the union and overlap of
author sets over time, in the spirit of Bandy & Diakopoulos (2021).
*Expected challenge:* third-party feed generators appear, disappear, and
error intermittently, so the collection design must treat missingness as
data (which feeds die?) rather than as a nuisance, and concentration
metrics must be compared at fixed sample sizes.

**2. Starter packs and network formation.** *Question:* does the initial
follow neighborhood a newcomer receives from a starter pack durably
shape the community they end up in, or does organic rewiring wash out
initial conditions? *Data:* a roster of active starter packs with join
counts; cohorts of recently created accounts whose first-day follows
closely match a pack's roster (a behavioral signature of joining through
it); repeated crawls of those accounts' follow graphs over subsequent
months using Part 03's methods. *Method:* community detection on the
evolving follow graph, comparing users seeded by different packs but
matched on join week and early activity; survival analysis of which
seeded follows persist versus get pruned. *Expected challenge:*
identification — who joins through which pack is not random (a
gardening pack recruits gardeners), so the design needs matched
comparisons and falsification tests, and the "joined via pack" inference
itself has measurement error worth validating.

**3. Labeler governance: do independent moderators agree?** *Question:*
how much do third-party labelers' decisions converge with the platform's
own moderation service, and where they diverge, in which direction?
*Data:* the public policy menus (`getServices`) of the Bluesky
Moderation Service and a roster of prominent third-party labelers;
labels queried from each labeler's own service endpoint (`queryLabels`
against each labeler's service URL) for a common random sample of
accounts and posts. *Method:* map each labeler's label values onto a
shared category scheme, then compute prevalence per labeler and
inter-labeler agreement (e.g., Cohen's κ) per category — a direct
empirical test of whether stackable moderation produces redundant or
genuinely plural governance. *Expected challenge:* labelers differ
wildly in scope, taxonomy, and uptime, so the category mapping is itself
a contestable research decision to document; and because labels are
accusations attached to identities, results must be reported strictly
in aggregate.
